questions.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
questions.problem: Use the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of $\sqrt{x}$ about $x=4$ to approximate the value of $\sqrt{\pi }.$ Give your answer to $4$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=4.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2} \\ f(4) & ={4}^{1/2}=2 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ {f}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{2}(4)^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{{2}^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}){x}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{″}(4) & =-\frac{1}{4}(4)^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{{2}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x} & =2+\frac{1}{{2}^{2}}(x-4)-\frac{1}{2!}(\frac{1}{{2}^{5}})(x-4)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =2+\frac{x-4}{4}-\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{64}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=\pi $ into the above to approximate $\sqrt{\pi }.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\pi } & ≈2+\frac{\pi -4}{4}-\frac{(\pi -4)^{2}}{64} \\  & =1.773\,9\,,\end{aligned}
$$

to $4$ decimal places.

questions.problem: Use the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)$ about $x=0$ to approximate the value of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.5).$ Give your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=0.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) \\ f(0) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{0+1}=1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(0) & =-\frac{1}{(0+1)^{2}}=-1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{2}{(x+1)^{3}} \\ {f}^{‴}(0) & =\frac{2}{(0+1)^{3}}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) & =(0)+(1)(x-0)+\frac{(-1)}{2!}(x-0)^{2}+\frac{(2)}{3!}(x-0)^{3}+⋯ \\  & =x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=0.5$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.5).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡1.5 & ≈(0.5)-\frac{1}{2}(0.5)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(0.5)^{3} \\  & =0.417\,,\end{aligned}
$$

to three decimal places.

questions.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and $a=\pi .$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x \\ f(\pi ) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\pi )=-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\pi ) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\pi )\operatorname{tan}⁡(\pi )=0 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x{tan}^{2}⁡x+{sec}^{3}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(\pi ) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\pi ){tan}^{2}⁡(\pi )+{sec}^{3}⁡(\pi )=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}⁡x & =-1+(0)(x-\pi )+\frac{(-1)}{2!}(x-\pi )^{2}+⋯ \\  & =-1-\frac{1}{2}(x-\pi )^{2}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=\pi +0.2$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{sec}⁡(\pi +0.2).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}⁡(\pi +0.2) & ≈-1-\frac{1}{2}{(\pi +0.2-\pi )}^{2} \\  & =-1-\frac{1}{2}(0.2)^{2} \\  & =-1-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{25}) \\  & =-1-\frac{1}{50} \\  & =-\frac{51}{50}.\end{aligned}
$$
